header.title: Architecting Autonomous Systems: Anatomy, Multi-Agent Topologies, and Enterprise Governance
header.subtitle: AI in 5 Days (DAY1) • Architect Track • For Rafee Mohamed

textParagraph.text: Transitioning from predictive machine learning models to autonomous agentic architectures requires reframing language models as probabilistic reasoning engines situated inside an iterative control loop: Get the Mission, Scan the Scene, Think, Act, and Observe. For enterprise architects, scaling beyond brittle single-agent scripts demands strict service decomposition into three foundational tiers: the reasoning Model (the brain), actionable Tools and interfaces (the hands), and a stateful Orchestration Layer (the nervous system) running atop production runtimes. As systems evolve from Level 1 connected problem-solvers to Level 3 collaborative multi-agent architectures, architects must design resilient interaction topologies (Coordinator, Sequential, and Iterative Refinement) governed by standardized protocols such as the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and Agent-to-Agent (A2A) with cryptographic Agent Cards. Operating fleets safely requires addressing agent sprawl through a centralized control plane comprising Agent Gateway for runtime policy enforcement and Model Armor sanitization, Agent Registry for discovery and versioning, SPIFFE-based Agent Identity principals for least-privilege delegation, and comprehensive OpenTelemetry trace instrumentation across stochastic execution trajectories.

decoratedText.text: Why do traditional OAuth user tokens and service account IAM roles fail when an autonomous agent delegates execution across a multi-tier agent chain, and how do SPIFFE-backed Agent Identities solve the delegation chain problem?

Draft an enterprise architecture boundary diagram and control policy for a financial reporting multi-agent workflow. Specify: 1) The distinct trust boundaries between User, Coordinator Agent, and Data Retrieval Tool; 2) The Agent Identity (SPIFFE ID) and least-privilege AuthZ constraints assigned to each agent principal; and 3) The inspection chokepoints where an Agent Gateway and Model Armor validate inputs and tool invocations before execution.
